Control? No, no, that's exactly the problem, Doctor. I really don't have any control at all. It's... well, let me try to explain it properly. You know, like I said, I'm a bookkeeper, so my whole life is about control and making sure everything balances out perfectly. Everything has a column, everything has a place. I mean, I know I have to be up early for work the next morning, and I know I don't need the food. But my hands... they just keep reaching for more. 

It's almost like I'm watching someone else do it. I just keep reaching into the bag, or opening another wrapper, and I can't stop. I'll just keep going and going until I feel so incredibly embarrassed and just... sick of myself. It's this terrible feeling, because normally I'm such a disciplined guy, you know? I pay my bills on time, I keep my house clean, but right then, sitting in the dark with all those wrappers, I just can't make myself stop no matter how hard I yell at myself in my head. I just keep eating until it's all gone.

Guilty? Oh, gosh... yes. Guilty doesn't even begin to cover it, Doctor. It's this heavy, sinking feeling right in the pit of my stomach. Like I said, I'm a numbers guy, right? I calculate things. Well, that's... gosh, that's a really good question, Doctor. I've thought about that a lot, actually. You see, the class itself—it's an advanced Excel certification course, you know, macros and pivot tables, that sort of thing—it's not really stressful. In fact, I actually enjoy it. I like the logic of it, the way everything has a formula and a result. So I wouldn't say I'm leaving the class feeling anxious or worked up about the material. It's not like my mind is racing about spreadsheets when I get in the car. 

But as for why it happens then... I just don't really know. I've tried to analyze it, like I would a ledger that's out of balance. I look for the trigger, you know? Is it because it's late? The class ends at 8:30 PM, so by the time I'm driving, it's dark, the streets are quiet. Maybe it's just the fact that the day is over and there's this... this void, I guess? Or maybe it's just the routine of driving past that particular fast-food place on the way back. I've even tried taking a different route home, going down Elm Street instead of the main avenue, but then I just end up stopping at the gas station on the corner and buying snacks there instead. 

So, I can't really put my finger on it being stress, or anxiety, or even just the time of day. It's more like... it's just this thing that happens now. Like a bad habit that's taken on a life of its own. I sit in the car, the engine running, and I tell myself, 'Arthur, just drive straight home. You have chicken in the fridge.' But then my blinker goes on, and I'm pulling into the drive-thru, and I don't even fully understand why I'm doing it. I wish I had a better answer for you, I really do, because if I knew why it was happening, maybe I could figure out how to stop it. But right now, I'm just... I'm really at a loss.

Emotions... well, that's... I mean, I've really tried to sit down and parse it out, you know? I'm driving, and then I'm eating, and the emotions—the terrible, overwhelming guilt and shame—they only show up *after* the fact. Beforehand? During? I really couldn't tell you that I'm feeling much of anything at all. It's incredibly frustrating not to have a neat little label to slap on it, like 'I eat because I'm sad.' I'd rinse my mouth out afterward and just stare at myself in the mirror, feeling even more pathetic than before. It's like a vicious cycle, you know? The eating makes me feel guilty, and the guilt makes me panic, and the panic makes me do... that. And then I just feel guilty all over again. I just want it to stop.\n\nDoctor: Do these episodes of eating happen when you're feeling stressed or anxious after the class, or is it more about the time of day or something else?\n\nPatient: Well, that's... gosh, that's a really good question, Doctor. I've thought about that a lot, actually. You see, the class itself—it's an advanced Excel certification course, you know, macros and pivot tables, that sort of thing—it's not really stressful. In fact, I actually enjoy it. I like the logic of it, the way everything has a formula and a result. So I wouldn't say I'm leaving the class feeling anxious or worked up about the material. It's not like my mind is racing about spreadsheets when I get in the car. \n\nBut as for why it happens then... I just don't really know. I've tried to analyze it, like I would a ledger that's out of balance. I look for the trigger, you know? Is it because it's late? The class ends at 8:30 PM, so by the time I'm driving, it's dark, the streets are quiet. Maybe it's just the fact that the day is over and there's this... this void, I guess? Or maybe it's just the routine of driving past that particular fast-food place on the way back. I've even tried taking a different route home, going down Elm Street instead of the main avenue, but then I just end up stopping at the gas station on the corner and buying snacks there instead. \n\nSo, I can't really put my finger on it being stress, or anxiety, or even just the time of day. It's more like... it's just this thing that happens now. Like a bad habit that's taken on a life of its own. I sit in the car, the engine running, and I tell myself, 'Arthur, just drive straight home. You have chicken in the fridge.' But then my blinker goes on, and I'm pulling into the drive-thru, and I don't even fully understand why I'm doing it. I wish I had a better answer for you, I really do, because if I knew why it was happening, maybe I could figure out how to stop it. But right now, I'm just... I'm really at a loss.\n\nDoctor: Do you think these episodes of eating are triggered by any specific emotions you're feeling at that time?\n\nPatient: Emotions... well, that's... I mean, I've really tried to sit down and parse it out, you know? Like I said, I like to balance the books, figure out where every cent goes, so I've tried to do that with my feelings, too. I've sat there with a cup of black coffee on a Sunday morning, just looking out the window at the neighbor's yard—they have this lovely oak tree that sheds leaves everywhere, which drives me a bit mad, but it's peaceful to look at—and I try to trace it back. I'm driving, and then I'm eating, and the emotions—the terrible, overwhelming guilt and shame—they only show up *after* the fact. Beforehand? During? I really couldn't tell you that I'm feeling much of anything at all. It's incredibly frustrating not to have a neat little label to slap on it, like 'I eat because I'm sad.' ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Hungry? Well, gosh, you'd think so, wouldn't you? It would certainly make the whole thing a lot easier to understand if I were just, you know, famished. But... no. No, I'm really not hungry at all. I've actually paid close attention to that, because I thought, 'Arthur, maybe you're just not eating enough during the day.' But I always make sure to have a proper, sensible dinner before I even leave the house for the community center. Right around 5:30, I'll sit down and have a baked chicken breast, maybe some steamed carrots or a little side salad with a light vinaigrette. Very measured, you know? Just enough to keep the engine running. 

So by the time 8:30 rolls around and I'm driving home, my stomach isn't rumbling. There are no hunger pangs. I'm not lightheaded or anything like that. In fact, most of the time I can still physically feel that I'm perfectly satisfied from dinner. But then I'm in that drive-thru line anyway, and I'm ordering... well, I'm ordering enough food for three grown men. And when I start eating it—the burgers, the fries, all of it—it's not because my body is asking for nourishment. It's not a physical need for fuel. 

It defies all logic, really. If you look at it like a balance sheet, there's absolutely no deficit that needs filling. The account is already full, so to speak. I'm not eating to satisfy a physical hunger. I'm just putting all that food into a stomach that doesn't even want it, which, frankly, just makes me feel even more foolish about the whole thing. It's just... I'm eating without needing to eat, and I just can't seem to stop myself once I start, even though I know I'm not hungry.

But I always make sure to have a proper, sensible dinner before I even leave the house for the community center. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
An emotional void? Gosh, I... I don't think so. That sounds a bit, well, a bit dramatic for someone like me, doesn't it? When I hear a phrase like 'emotional void,' I think of, oh, I don't know, a character in a Russian novel, or maybe someone on one of those afternoon talk shows. My sister Brenda watches those sometimes when she's doing her ironing, and they're always talking about 'filling the void' and 'healing your inner child' and all that sort of thing. But I just don't see myself in that language at all. 

If you look at my life, Doctor, it's really quite full. Not in a flashy way, mind you. I don't go skydiving or travel to Europe or anything extravagant. But I have my job at the firm, I have my routines, my Excel class at the community center, my Sunday mornings with the newspaper and the coffee... The ledger of my life is, well, it's balanced. I don't feel like there's some gaping hole in the middle of it all that needs patching up. 

I mean, if I had a void, wouldn't I feel it during the day? When I'm at the office tallying up the quarterly expenses for Mr. Henderson, or when I'm at the grocery store picking out my chicken breasts for the week? But I don't. I feel perfectly fine. Content, even. I like my quiet life. 

So when I'm in that drive-thru, it's not like I'm trying to shovel french fries into some big, dark, emotional black hole. It really isn't. Like I was trying to explain earlier with the emotions, there's just... nothing. No sadness, no emptiness, no void. It's just the driving, and the ordering, and the chewing. I really wish I could give you a better answer, because 'filling a void' sounds like a very neat, logical explanation, doesn't it? It sounds like something we could write down on a chart and figure out a step-by-step plan to fix. But if I'm being completely honest with you, and with myself, I just don't feel empty at all before I start eating. I just feel... bewildered by the whole routine, really.

It's not like my mind is racing about spreadsheets when I get in the car. \n\nBut as for why it happens then... I just don't really know. I've tried to analyze it, like I would a ledger that's out of balance. I look for the trigger, you know? Is it because it's late? The class ends at 8:30 PM, so by the time I'm driving, it's dark, the streets are quiet. Maybe it's just the fact that the day is over and there's this... this void, I guess? Or maybe it's just the routine of driving past that particular fast-food place on the way back. I've even tried taking a different route home, going down Elm Street instead of the main avenue, but then I just end up stopping at the gas station on the corner and buying snacks there instead. \n\nSo, I can't really put my finger on it being stress, or anxiety, or even just the time of day. It's more like... it's just this thing that happens now. Like a bad habit that's taken on a life of its own. I sit in the car, the engine running, and I tell myself, 'Arthur, just drive straight home. You have chicken in the fridge.' But then my blinker goes on, and I'm pulling into the drive-thru, and I don't even fully understand why I'm doing it. I wish I had a better answer for you, I really do, because if I knew why it was happening, maybe I could figure out how to stop it. But right now, I'm just... I'm really at a loss.\n\nDoctor: Do you think these episodes of eating are triggered by any specific emotions you're feeling at that time?\n\nPatient: Emotions... well, that's... I mean, I've really tried to sit down and parse it out, you know? Like I said, I like to balance the books, figure out where every cent goes, so I've tried to do that with my feelings, too. I've sat there with a cup of black coffee on a Sunday morning, just looking out the window at the neighbor's yard—they have this lovely oak tree that sheds leaves everywhere, which drives me a bit mad, but it's peaceful to look at—and I try to trace it back. Unfulfilled? Dissatisfied? Oh, my goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. I know some people might look at a life like mine—fifty-five years old, working the same bookkeeping job for going on twenty years, taking a Tuesday night Excel class just to keep the skills sharp—and they might think, 'Well, Arthur, isn't that a bit dull?' But I don't find it dull in the slightest. I actually find a great deal of comfort in predictability. 

I like knowing that on Mondays, I review the payroll accounts for Mr. Henderson. I like knowing that on Thursdays, I go to the supermarket and buy my groceries for the week, always parking in the same section of the lot, if I can help it. It's... well, it's organized. It's neat. Everything has its proper place. I've never been one of those fellows who needs to be constantly entertained or, you know, chasing the next big thrill. I have my little apartment, I have my routines. And that, to me, is a perfectly fine way to spend a morning. I'm very satisfied with it, really.

Which is exactly why this whole... this whole drive-thru business after my class is just so completely maddening!

I could look at the situation and say, 'Ah, Arthur, you're unhappy with your daily lot, and that's why you're doing this.' It would be a logical cause and effect. But I'm *not* unhappy. I'm quite satisfied with my routine. I like my life exactly the way it is. So doing all this... it just doesn't make a lick of sense, Doctor. It really, truly doesn't.

Oh, absolutely. That is... well, that is the crux of the whole bizarre situation, Doctor. It's exactly like doing something I don't want to be doing. I mean, it's not like I'm sleepwalking, you know? I'm completely awake. I'm sitting there, usually in the driver's seat, or sometimes I've brought the haul inside to the little table in my kitchen, and my brain is entirely aware of what's happening. I can see the clock on the microwave or the dashboard, I know I have to be up at 6:15 the next morning to get to the office, and my mind is just begging me to stop. 

I'll buy these things—sometimes it's the drive-thru, or sometimes I'll stop at the 24-hour pharmacy on the way back from the community center and get these big bags of chips or those little powdered donuts—and once I start on those snacks, I keep telling myself to close the bag and go to bed. I mean, I will literally have a full, rational conversation with myself in my head. I'll think, 'Arthur, just fold the top of the bag over. Put it down. Go inside, brush your teeth, and go to sleep.' It’s a very simple, logical directive. 

But... it's like there's a complete disconnect between management and the workers on the floor, if you catch my drift. I give the order to stop, but my hands just keep reaching for more. My brain says 'halt,' but my hand goes right back into the bag, pulls out another handful, and then I'm chewing and swallowing, and then the hand goes right back in again. I just sit there watching myself do it, completely unable to hit the brakes. It goes against every sensible bone in my body. 

And it just goes on and on like that until every last crumb is gone. And then... well, then the dust settles, and I just feel so terribly embarrassed and sick of myself. I sit there looking at the empty wrappers, feeling physically uncomfortable, of course, but mostly just sick with myself over the sheer lack of discipline. I think, 'You didn't even want to eat this, so why on earth did you just do it?' It's humiliating, really, to be a fifty-five-year-old man who can balance a million-dollar ledger but can't even tell his own hands to stop moving.

I don't know, I'll stop for food on the drive home, which sounds normal enough, right? But I end up ordering and eating a completely full fast-food meal. And then, it's like a switch flips or something. I'll hit the vending machine and get a bunch of candy, just whatever is in there, and eat all of that too. And then I finally get home, and I'm still not done. I'll just keep going, tearing into more snacks at the house, just whatever I can find in the pantry or the fridge. \n\nIt’s honestly like... it's like I am making up for the whole entire day all at once. I just sit there afterward looking at all the wrappers and I don't even know how it happened, but it just keeps happening after these evening classes, and I just... I really don't know what to do about it anymore. It's really been weighing on my mind.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're in control of your eating during these episodes after class?\n\nPatient: Control? No, no, that's exactly the problem, Doctor. I really don't have any control at all. It's... well, let me try to explain it properly. You know, like I said, I'm a bookkeeper, so my whole life is about control and making sure everything balances out perfectly. Everything has a column, everything has a place. But during these... these times after class, it's completely different. \n\nI'll get home, and I usually sit down at the kitchen island—sometimes I don't even bother turning on the main overhead lights, just the little one over the stove—and once I start on those snacks, it's like my brain and my body just disconnect from each other. I'll be sitting there, and I keep telling myself, 'Okay, that's enough now, just close the bag, put a clip on it, and go up to bed.' I mean, I know I have to be up early for work the next morning, and I know I don't need the food. But my hands... they just keep reaching for more. \n\nIt's almost like I'm watching someone else do it. I just keep reaching into the bag, or opening another wrapper, and I can't stop. I'll just keep going and going until I feel so incredibly embarrassed and just... sick of myself. It's this terrible feeling, because normally I'm such a disciplined guy, you know? I pay my bills on time, I keep my house clean, but right then, sitting in the dark with all those wrappers, I just can't make myself stop no matter how hard I yell at myself in my head. I just keep eating until it's all gone.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel guilty after these eating episodes are over?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Oh, gosh... yes. Guilty doesn't even begin to cover it, Doctor. It's this heavy, sinking feeling right in the pit of my stomach. Like I said, I'm a numbers guy, right? I calculate things. So I sit there, looking at the empty wrappers—the fast food bags, the candy wrappers from the vending machine, the empty chip bags from the pantry—and my brain just starts adding up the calories, the fat, the sheer volume of what I just put into my body. And the guilt is just... it's suffocating. \n\nI start thinking about my waistline, about how I'm 55 and my metabolism isn't what it used to be. I think about having to buy new trousers for work, going up a size, and how humiliated I'd feel. The fear of all that food just turning into fat and showing on me... it gets so overwhelming. And, well, I haven't told anyone this part, not a single soul, because it's just so shameful for a man my age... but a few times, maybe three or four times after those really bad late-night eating spells, the guilt and the panic got so bad that I... I went into the bathroom. \n\nI turned on the faucet so it would be loud, just in case, even though I live alone. And I stood over the toilet and I... I made myself throw up. I just couldn't bear the thought of all that food sitting inside me, ruining everything, making me gain weight. It's awful, it really is. I'd rinse my mouth out afterward and just stare at myself in the mirror, feeling even more pathetic than before. It's like a vicious cycle, you know? The eating makes me feel guilty, and the guilt makes me panic, and the panic makes me do... that. And then I just feel guilty all over again. I just want it to stop.\n\nDoctor: Do these episodes of eating happen when you're feeling stressed or anxious after the class, or is it more about the time of day or something else?\n\nPatient: Well, that's... gosh, that's a really good question, Doctor. I've thought about that a lot, actually. You see, the class itself—it's an advanced Excel certification course, you know, macros and pivot tables, that sort of thing—it's not really stressful. In fact, I actually enjoy it. I like the logic of it, the way everything has a formula and a result. So I wouldn't say I'm leaving the class feeling anxious or worked up about the material. It's not like my mind is racing about spreadsheets when I get in the car. \n\nBut as for why it happens then... I just don't really know. I've tried to analyze it, like I would a ledger that's out of balance. I look for the trigger, you know? Is it because it's late? The class ends at 8:30 PM, so by the time I'm driving, it's dark, the streets are quiet. Maybe it's just the fact that the day is over and there's this... this void, I guess? Or maybe it's just the routine of driving past that particular fast-food place on the way back. I've even tried taking a different route home, going down Elm Street instead of the main avenue, but then I just end up stopping at the gas station on the corner and buying snacks there instead. \n\nSo, I can't really put my finger on it being stress, or anxiety, or even just the time of day. It's more like... it's just this thing that happens now. Like a bad habit that's taken on a life of its own. I sit in the car, the engine running, and I tell myself, 'Arthur, just drive straight home. You have chicken in the fridge.' But then my blinker goes on, and I'm pulling into the drive-thru, and I don't even fully understand why I'm doing it. I wish I had a better answer for you, I really do, because if I knew why it was happening, maybe I could figure out how to stop it. But right now, I'm just... I'm really at a loss.\n\nDoctor: Do you think these episodes of eating are triggered by any specific emotions you're feeling at that time?\n\nPatient: Emotions... well, that's... I mean, I've really tried to sit down and parse it out, you know? Like I said, I like to balance the books, figure out where every cent goes, so I've tried to do that with my feelings, too. I've sat there with a cup of black coffee on a Sunday morning, just looking out the window at the neighbor's yard—they have this lovely oak tree that sheds leaves everywhere, which drives me a bit mad, but it's peaceful to look at—and I try to trace it back. I ask myself, 'Arthur, were you sad? Were you angry? Were you lonely?' \n\nAnd... honestly, Doctor, I come up empty. I really do. It's not like I'm sitting in the car crying over a lost love or fuming because my boss, Mr. Henderson, made a passive-aggressive comment about my filing system. It's not like that at all. It's almost an absence of emotion, if that makes any sense? It's just this... this blankness. I'm driving, the radio is on—usually just the local news or classical music, nothing that gets the blood pumping—and there's no big emotional wave crashing over me. \n\nI've read articles, you know, in those magazines at the dentist's office, about emotional eating. About people who eat a whole cake because they're heartbroken or stressed about a mortgage payment. But I just don't fit that mold. I don't feel a sudden spike of sadness or a sudden rush of anxiety right before I pull into the drive-thru. It's just... I'm driving, and then I'm eating, and the emotions—the terrible, overwhelming guilt and shame—they only show up *after* the fact. Beforehand? During? I really couldn't tell you that I'm feeling much of anything at all. It's incredibly frustrating not to have a neat little label to slap on it, like 'I eat because I'm sad.' I wish it were that simple.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel hungry when you start eating after the class?\n\nPatient: Hungry? Well, gosh, you'd think so, wouldn't you? I've actually paid close attention to that, because I thought, 'Arthur, maybe you're just not eating enough during the day.' But I always make sure to have a proper, sensible dinner before I even leave the house for the community center. Right around 5:30, I'll sit down and have a baked chicken breast, maybe some steamed carrots or a little side salad with a light vinaigrette. Very measured, you know? And when I start eating it—the burgers, the fries, all of it—it's not because my body is asking for nourishment. It's not a physical need for fuel. \n\nIt defies all logic, really. If you look at it like a balance sheet, there's absolutely no deficit that needs filling. The account is already full, so to speak. I'm not eating to satisfy a physical hunger. I'm just putting all that food into a stomach that doesn't even want it, which, frankly, just makes me feel even more foolish about the whole thing. It's just... I'm eating without needing to eat, and I just can't seem to stop myself once I start, even though I know I'm not hungry.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel any sense of pleasure while eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: Pleasure? Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't call it pleasure at all. I mean, I know what pleasure from food is supposed to feel like. My sister, Brenda, she makes this absolutely phenomenal strawberry rhubarb pie every Thanksgiving. She uses just the right amount of sugar so it's still got that tart bite to it, you know? And when I have a slice of that, sitting in her dining room with a cup of decaf coffee, that is pleasure. You savor a thing like that. You take a little bite with your fork and you think, 'Wow, this is truly delicious.' \n\nBut this... what happens in the car after my Excel class? There's no savoring. There's no culinary appreciation whatsoever. Honestly, Doctor, I'm eating it so fast I barely even taste it half the time. It's just... chewing and swallowing, chewing and swallowing. Like a machine processing a stack of invoices. Just getting through the pile. \n\nSometimes I'll buy these double cheeseburgers from the drive-thru, and you'd look at that and think, 'Well, Arthur, you must really love cheeseburgers to be buying three of them at once.' But I don't even really like them that much! The buns are usually a bit soggy from the steam in the wrapper, and the cheese is that highly processed stuff that just sort of glues itself to the roof of your mouth. But I just keep eating them anyway. It’s almost like the food is just... material. Just inventory to be moved. \n\nSo, no, there’s no joy in it. No pleasure. It’s not some special treat I’m giving myself after a long day. If anything, it feels like work. I almost wish it *were* pleasurable, because maybe then it would make a lick of sense on some basic human level, you know? Seeking pleasure is something you can put on a balance sheet. But doing this, getting no joy out of it, and feeling terrible afterward? My sister Brenda watches those sometimes when she's doing her ironing, and they're always talking about 'filling the void' and 'healing your inner child' and all that sort of thing. But I just don't see myself in that language at all. \n\nIf you look at my life, Doctor, it's really quite full. Not in a flashy way, mind you. I don't go skydiving or travel to Europe or anything extravagant. But I have my job at the firm, I have my routines, my Excel class at the community center, my Sunday mornings with the newspaper and the coffee... The ledger of my life is, well, it's balanced. I don't feel like there's some gaping hole in the middle of it all that needs patching up. \n\nI mean, if I had a void, wouldn't I feel it during the day? When I'm at the office tallying up the quarterly expenses for Mr. Henderson, or when I'm at the grocery store picking out my chicken breasts for the week? But I don't. I feel perfectly fine. Content, even. I like my quiet life. \n\nSo when I'm in that drive-thru, it's not like I'm trying to shovel french fries into some big, dark, emotional black hole. It really isn't. How often? Well, let me think. The advanced Excel course—the one at the community center I was telling you about—runs for a full sixteen weeks. We started back in early September, right after Labor Day, when the weather was still quite warm. But this... this whole drive-thru and snacking business didn't start on day one. No, I'd say it's been going on for about the past three months. Right around the time we got into macros and VLOOKUPs, actually. Not that the coursework itself is stressing me out, you understand, I quite enjoy the formulas. But for about the past three months, it's become a rather grim little routine. 

It doesn't happen every single day, thank goodness. I don't think my checking account could handle that, let alone my pride. But there has usually been at least one night each week, almost always right after that class, when I overeat like that. I'll just completely lose control of the steering wheel, so to speak, and consume all those burgers or entire bags of donuts in one sitting. 

And... well. There is one other part of it, Doctor. Something I haven't quite brought myself to mention yet, because, frankly, it's the most shameful part of the whole equation. After I eat all of that, when the dust settles and I'm sitting there looking at the wrappers, feeling so dreadfully full and sick with myself... I go into the bathroom. And I... I make myself throw up afterward. 

I know, I know how it sounds. A man of my age, fifty-five years old, leaning over a toilet bowl. It's absolutely mortifying. I'm driving, the radio is on—usually just the local news or classical music, nothing that gets the blood pumping—and there's no big emotional wave crashing over me. \n\nI've read articles, you know, in those magazines at the dentist's office, about emotional eating. About people who eat a whole cake because they're heartbroken or stressed about a mortgage payment. But I just don't fit that mold. I don't feel a sudden spike of sadness or a sudden rush of anxiety right before I pull into the drive-thru. It's just... I'm driving, and then I'm eating, and the emotions—the terrible, overwhelming guilt and shame—they only show up *after* the fact. Beforehand? During? I really couldn't tell you that I'm feeling much of anything at all. It's incredibly frustrating not to have a neat little label to slap on it, like 'I eat because I'm sad.' I wish it were that simple.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel hungry when you start eating after the class?\n\nPatient: Hungry? Well, gosh, you'd think so, wouldn't you? It would certainly make the whole thing a lot easier to understand if I were just, you know, famished. But... no. No, I'm really not hungry at all. I've actually paid close attention to that, because I thought, 'Arthur, maybe you're just not eating enough during the day.' But I always make sure to have a proper, sensible dinner before I even leave the house for the community center. Right around 5:30, I'll sit down and have a baked chicken breast, maybe some steamed carrots or a little side salad with a light vinaigrette. Very measured, you know? Just enough to keep the engine running. \n\nSo by the time 8:30 rolls around and I'm driving home, my stomach isn't rumbling. There are no hunger pangs. I'm not lightheaded or anything like that. In fact, most of the time I can still physically feel that I'm perfectly satisfied from dinner. But then I'm in that drive-thru line anyway, and I'm ordering... well, I'm ordering enough food for three grown men. And when I start eating it—the burgers, the fries, all of it—it's not because my body is asking for nourishment. It's not a physical need for fuel. \n\nIt defies all logic, really. If you look at it like a balance sheet, there's absolutely no deficit that needs filling. The account is already full, so to speak. I'm not eating to satisfy a physical hunger. I'm just putting all that food into a stomach that doesn't even want it, which, frankly, just makes me feel even more foolish about the whole thing. It's just... I'm eating without needing to eat, and I just can't seem to stop myself once I start, even though I know I'm not hungry.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel any sense of pleasure while eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: Pleasure? Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't call it pleasure at all. I mean, I know what pleasure from food is supposed to feel like. And when I have a slice of that, sitting in her dining room with a cup of decaf coffee, that is pleasure. You savor a thing like that. You take a little bite with your fork and you think, 'Wow, this is truly delicious.' \n\nBut this... what happens in the car after my Excel class? There's no savoring. But I don't even really like them that much! The buns are usually a bit soggy from the steam in the wrapper, and the cheese is that highly processed stuff that just sort of glues itself to the roof of your mouth. But I just keep eating them anyway. It’s almost like the food is just... material. Just inventory to be moved. \n\nSo, no, there’s no joy in it. No pleasure. It’s not some special treat I’m giving myself after a long day. If anything, it feels like work. It's just this frantic, messy task I feel compelled to get through before I can go home, throw the wrappers deep in the outside trash can so the neighbors don't see, and then face the guilt of it all. I almost wish it *were* pleasurable, because maybe then it would make a lick of sense on some basic human level, you know? Seeking pleasure is something you can put on a balance sheet. But doing this, getting no joy out of it, and feeling terrible afterward? It just completely defies reason.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're trying to fill an emotional void when you eat after the class?\n\nPatient: An emotional void? Gosh, I... I don't think so. That sounds a bit, well, a bit dramatic for someone like me, doesn't it? When I hear a phrase like 'emotional void,' I think of, oh, I don't know, a character in a Russian novel, or maybe someone on one of those afternoon talk shows. My sister Brenda watches those sometimes when she's doing her ironing, and they're always talking about 'filling the void' and 'healing your inner child' and all that sort of thing. A deeper psychological issue... well. I'm not a psychiatrist, Doctor, so I don't know if I'd use the word 'deeper,' as if it's some sort of repressed childhood memory or anything out of a movie. But... I suppose there is something fundamental about how I view myself that gets... derailed. Completely derailed. 

You see, I’ve been a bookkeeper for three decades. Precision, discipline, carefulness—those aren't just job requirements for me. That is who I am. I pride myself on being a man who has his house in order, someone who doesn't make sloppy mistakes. But... and this is the part that is so incredibly frustrating to admit... all of that pride, all of that identity, is completely fragile. It all hinges on my waistline. 

For example, I'll get up in the morning, shower, shave, and go to put on my clothes for work. If I put on my dress shirt and it feels even slightly tight around my middle... it just shatters me. It's not just a passing thought of, 'Oh, I should eat a salad for lunch.' No, it's a profound, overwhelming sense of defeat. On days my shirt feels tight around my middle, I feel like I have completely failed at being the careful, disciplined person I try so hard to be. It’s as if that one physical flaw negates everything else about my character. 

I can go into the office and do a brilliant job—the rest of my bookkeeping work can be absolutely flawless, not a single penny off in the ledgers, balancing accounts that would make a junior clerk weep—but it brings me no satisfaction. None at all. Because underneath my suit jacket, I know the shirt is pulling, and that tightness means I am undisciplined. It means I am a fraud. It's all I can think about while I'm sitting at my desk. So, if tying your entire sense of self-worth and morality to how your clothes fit is a psychological issue, then... yes. I suppose it very much is.

Binge eating... well, I suppose that’s the word for it, isn't it? It sounds so dramatic, like something you'd hear on a television program, but... if I really sit down and analyze the mechanics of what happens when I get home, maybe it is.

    ]
  }
}
